title: Temperature-dependent ice-nucleating activity of wintertime urban PM 2.5 : chemical signatures and estimated source contributions
content: Urban PM2.5 contains chemically diverse particle populations whose relationships with ice-nucleating particle (INP) concentrations may vary with freezing temperature. We measured immersion-freezing INP number concentrations (NINP) in wintertime PM2.5 collected in Xi'an during dust, fireworks, clean, and polluted periods and examined their associations with aerosol chemical composition and sources. Median freezing temperatures (T50) differed significantly among the four conditions (p < 0.001), ranging from −14.3 °C during dust events to −20.0 °C during fireworks periods. Polluted samples had significantly warmer T50 values than clean samples, although differences in NINP at individual temperatures were not statistically significant. Heat treatment revealed a substantial heat-labile fraction (84.9%) in dust samples at −12.5 °C. Mineral- and metal-related elements showed persistent positive associations with NINP, with Mn, Ti, and Fe ranking among the leading random forest predictors at −17.5 and −19.0 °C. Secondary inorganic ions and selected organic aerosol factors were also positively associated with NINP, particularly at colder temperatures. Positive matrix factorization combined with temperature-specific regression attributed the largest estimated source contribution to fugitive dust at −14.5 °C (77.2%) and vehicle emissions at −17.5 °C (52.7%). At −20.5 °C, coal combustion (35.4%), fugitive dust (29.5%), and industrial emissions (29.4%) made comparable estimated contributions. The temperature-dependent chemical and source associations reveal differences in the ice-nucleating characteristics of urban PM2.5 that are not represented by particle mass alone.
